KANNALAND RAPIST MAYOR

By: Latashia Naidoo | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Unique Selling Point:
As South Africa heads toward another local election, this story shows what’s truly at stake: not just ballots, but belief in the power of accountability.


Summary:
In December 2022, Carte Blanche exposed Kannaland’s scandal-plagued mayor Jeffrey Donson - a convicted child rapist who, despite national outrage, continued to hold public office.
Three years later, he’s still there.

Convicted in 2008 of statutory rape and indecent assault of a 15-year-old girl while serving as Oudtshoorn’s mayor, Donson has worn the mayoral chain three separate times - before his conviction, again in 2021, and once more in October 2022, just months before our exposé aired.
Public pressure forced his temporary removal in January 2022, but coalition politics between ICOSA and the ANCbrought him back.
In October 2023, ICOSA suspended him for “gross misconduct and bringing the party into disrepute.”
But within weeks, Donson reasserted control - and remains Executive Mayor of Kannaland in 2025.

Now, Action Society is pushing for a constitutional amendment to bar convicted sexual offenders from public office - what activists call “the Donson Clause.”

October 2025: IDonson remains mayor despite his 2008 conviction and failed suspension.
Action Society campaign: Renewed national call to change eligibility laws.
Upcoming elections: With local government polls looming in 2026, Donson’s case epitomises the collapse of accountability in local politics.
Political stakes: Parties that once backed him - or stayed silent - will now have to answer to voters.
National relevance: In a country that preaches “zero tolerance” for GBV, a convicted rapist’s survival in politics exposes the emptiness of that promise.

This story isn’t about one small-town scandal - it’s about a democracy without moral guardrails.
If a convicted child rapist can outlast exposure, suspension, and scandal - and still run a municipality - what does that say about the system itself?
Taxpayers pay his salary.
Survivors see justice mocked.
Voters are asked to choose between ethics and apathy.

As South Africa heads toward another local election, this story shows what’s truly at stake: not just ballots, but belief in the power of accountability.

Press Release:


Politics Without Consequence
Nearly three years ago, Carte Blanche exposed a convicted child rapist holding public office as executive mayor of a small town. Three years later, not much has changed. Convicted in 2008 of statutory rape and indecent assault, he’s been elected three separate times. And despite public pressure, suspensions and removals simply haven’t stuck. Meanwhile, this small town holds a dubious title: it's the Western Cape's worst-performing municipality. Now, activists are pushing for a constitutional amendment to bar convicted sexual offenders from public office. As the country heads toward another local election, it’s more than ballots at stake: it’s belief in the power of accountability.
Producer: Latashia Naidoo | Presenter: Govan Whittles

Script:


KANNALAND RAPIST MAYOR - FINAL:

VIZ: ARCHIVE (2022 confrontation)
MASA: ‘Nice to meet you, my name is Masa.’
JEFFREY DONSON: “Wat weet jy van morals? Jy kan nie vir my kom vir morals! You stole our land and you want to teach me about morals? No man, you can’t teach me about morals.”
MASA: We're talking about the 15-year-old that you had raped.
GOVAN: In 2022, we questioned a Klein Karoo mayor about his conviction for statutory rape.
JEFFREY DONSON: ‘All I’m doing is working for the community, and I am only doing my job.’
MASA: ‘You're still a convicted child rapist.

GOVAN: He insisted we leave.

JEFFREY DONSON: ‘I know what I know, and the community knows. Because they were in court.’

GOVAN LINK:
“Three years ago we confronted the Kannaland Municipality Mayor - a convicted child rapist who refused to answer for his past.
He was defiant then; three years later, he’s still here.”

GOVAN: He’s here because of a loophole in our law giving him access to public office - despite mounting calls for intervention.

KAYLYNN PALM: “It is unacceptable that we are allowing this man, after we know that he had raped - someone, he can come into office, walk into office- and think it’s fine to just run for office.”

GOVAN: “It’s clear from his social media, how he earned that nickname.”

GOVAN: Kannaland now ranks as the Western Cape’s worst-performing municipality. So we went back to ask why Jeffrey Donson is still in charge.

GOVAN: Kannaland covers Ladismith, Zoar, Calitzdorp and Van Wyksdorp - about 27 000 residents living through decades of decline.

GOVAN: In 2023, National Treasury imposed a Financial Recovery Plan on Kannaland. Council signed it off in August this year, but the municipality under Donson remains ‘technically insolvent’.

GOVAN: 17 years ago, while mayor of Kannaland, Donson was convicted of the statutory rape of a 15-year-old girl. He received a suspended sentence, meaning he remained eligible for public office.

GOVAN: He runs Kannaland through his own party, ICOSA, having been elected three times – all while surviving council battles, and even a suspension by ICOSA itself.

GOVAN: All this while the municipality continues its steady decline. It’s why we’ve come back three years later.

JOSLYN JOHNSON: “In 2022 I think, there was also a cry out from the public that he must be removed from Council or from the position as mayor, which happened…

GOVAN: In Zoar, we meet former DA Councilor and long-time resident, Jocelyn Johnson.

JOSLYN JOHNSON: “…but it only lasted for 8 months and then again there was a motion of no confidence and the the current mayor was then reelected as the mayor.”

GOVAN: Conditions in Zoar, like so many other small towns in the municipality, are dire. Johnson says spending decisions are based on politics rather than need.

JOSLYN JOHNSON: “The most money that Kannaland is spending money on now is on salaries instead of service delivery.”
JOSLYN JOHNSON: “The municipality currently has a deficit of R60 million towards their budget. But the employee-related ratio is currently at 66%.
So things doesn’t add up.”

GOVAN: That deficit means two-thirds of the budget is swallowed by salaries, and there isn’t enough left to fix pipes, roads, or basic services.

GOVAN: And despite looming local government elections, Joslyn fears nothing will change.

GOVAN: “Is Jeffrey Donson a popular person around here?”
JOSLYN JOHNSON: ‘I think his pro-poor political thinking is what get people attached to him.’
JOSLYN JOHNSON: “People should really go back to the drawing board come 2026, because if Kannaland can have another 5 years under this kind of administration…”
GOVAN: “You mean he might come back again?”
JOSLYN JOHNSON: “The possibility, yes.”

GOVAN LINK: “To many Kannaland residents, Jeffrey Donson isn’t the disgrace outsiders see; he’s part of the community. And in a town where loyalty shapes politics, maybe that’s what’s keeping him in power.”

GOVAN: But it’s not loyalty alone… he’s eligible through a legal loophole.

MASA: ‘The fact that you are standing as a mayor, and you are convicted of child rape…’
JEFFREY DONSON: “Why can’t I be mayor? Show me the law!”
MASA: ‘It’s still outrageous!’
JEFFREY DONSON: “Bring the law that says I can’t be mayor!”

GOVAN: That law - set out in the Constitution and the Municipal Structures Act - disqualifies candidates only when they’ve served more than 12 months in prison without a fine. It applies to statutory rape cases, too.

GOVAN: According to the IEC, Donson’s suspended sentence keeps him eligible - as mayor of the worst run municipality in the Western Cape.

GOVAN: Engineer Jan-Dirk Brak moved to Ladismith from Cape Town in 2019, looking for a quieter life. Instead, he found a municipality in crisis.

GOVAN: “I haven’t seen any municipal leadership or even municipal trucks since the whole day that we’ve been here.”
JAN-DIRK BRAK: “So when there’s a callout for a leaky pipe or a power failure or a burst pipe somewhere, in a bunch of cases people have to go and fetch the municipal workers from the facility and take them to the site to fix it.”
GOVAN: “Who has to fetch?”
JAN-DIRK BRAK: “The business owner or the person living in the house with the problem.”
GOVAN: “Has to fetch the municipal worker?”
JAN-DIRK BRAK: “Has to go fetch the people from the yard to come do the work…”
GOVAN: “Man!”
JAN-DIRK BRAK: “And then they’ll pitch up without the required equipment or PPE… it’s not the ampenaar se skuld nie… they don’t have the vehicles or the equipment or the pipe fittings.”
GOVAN: Residents are now paying for infrastructure repairs themselves.
JAN-DIRK BRAK: “So we had a massive problem with burst pipes about two months ago, and all the fittings were bought by the people in town and donated to the ampenare… because the municipality doesn’t have the money to buy the fittings and the screws and the sealants or whatever’s needed to fix the pipes.”

GOVAN: In a province where most municipalities achieved clean or stable audits, Kannaland is the outlier - the worst performer of all 24, with broken finances and collapsing services.

GOVAN: Yet even when faced with such obvious decay, why does the broader Kannaland community continue to stand with Donson?

GOVAN LINK
“Here in Ladismith they didn’t just re-elect Jeffrey Donson; they named a street after him.
A convicted child rapist - immortalised in metal and paint.”

GOVAN: In Kannaland, voter turnout is shrinking with each election cycle; a small but steady base keeps returning the same result.

GOVAN: To them, Donson is the mayor who dances with locals, and feels less like a politician and more like ‘ons se men’s’.”

GOVAN: “It‘s Day 2 in Ladismith, Kannaland, and we’re still looking for Jeffrey Donson. We haven’t been able to find him so far, and he’s not responding to our requests for an interview. This is where we spoke to him last time; I’m gonna go try and find him.”

GOVAN: “Middag. Howzit, howzit, hey howzit. Is the Mayor in today?”
BODYGUARD: “He’s not going to see anyone, he’s busy.”
GOVAN: “Sorry?”
BODYGUARD: “He doesn’t want to see anybody today.”
GOVAN: “Can you tell him that Govan from Carte Blanche is here. We have sent him a number of requests to speak to him.”
BODYGUARD: “He doesn’t want to speak to anybody.”
GOVAN: “He’s not going to speak to anybody? Can you tell him that we’re here though, just so that he knows we’re here? Just ask him to come and speak to us, we, we, we’re outside.”
BODYGUARD: Ja, but he's not going to see anybody today.
GOVAN: “Can you ask him to respond to our emails?”
BODYGUARD: “Okay, I will tell his PA now.”
(inaudible)
GOVAN: “So, hy is hier so? Hy is maar hy wil nie saam met ons wil praat?”
BODYGUARD: (inaudible)
GOVAN: “Okay, dankie.”

GOVAN: “Okay, well, that was his bodyguard. He says the Mayor knows we’re here, but has decided he’s not going to speak to anyone today, especially us. He says he doesn’t wanna see us or speak to us. This is the mayor of the worst municipality in the Western Cape, a convicted child rapist. And again, it’s ‘no comment’. It’s unacceptable!”

GOVAN: And that’s why there are mounting calls for reform.

KAYLYNN PALM: “Look, the voters, I think that they are partly to blame in terms of getting him into power, into this position, continuously….

GOVAN: Kaylynn Palm is from Action Society, a civil rights organisation fighting for a reformed justice system.

KAYLYNN PALM: “We also question, not only the voters, but also his colleagues in office. Why do they continuously vote him into stand for, for, for his position?”

GOVAN: Action Society wants to keep people with serious convictions - like Donson - out of public office. That means changing the law.

GOVAN: “What’s the campaign that Action Society launched?”
KAYLYNN PALM: “The campaign focussed on changing legislation
which focuses on people who come into office that have a history of serious crimes.”

GOVAN: “I’ve heard it being described as the ‘Donson Clause’…”
KAYLYNN PALM: “Absolutely, and that is something that we would like to zoom into and have changed, that amendment changed.”

GOVAN: Until that happens, Donson is entitled to serve as mayor. Kaylynn says that’s a dangerous message to be sending to victims.

KAYLYNN PALM: “I think it’s a smack in the face, and it’s a middle finger to people who are seeking justice for crimes like rape, crimes like sexual assault or GBV.”

KAYLYNN PALM: “I’m not sure if he’s just delusional, or if he just, he thinks people must forget what he did. But we can’t forget that he raped a child.”-

GOVAN: This story isn’t just about Jeffrey Donson. It’s about a system of public service unable to hold him to account, and a community of close to 30 thousand paying the price.

FTB.

GOVAN: In this Klein Karoo municipality, a convicted sex offender is still in office - shielded by silence, and the law.
KAYLYNN PALM: “I’m not sure if he’s just delusional, or if he thinks people must forget what he did. But we can’t forget that he raped a child, it was a child.”
GOVAN: We uncover how he stays in power - and why accountability never reaches Kannaland.

Promo link 2:
GOVAN: In this Klein Karoo municipality, a convicted sex offender is still running the show - while the town around him falls apart.
JOSLYN JOHNSON: “To be honest, I think the most money that Kannaland is spending on now is salaries - instead of service delivery.”
GOVAN: We investigate how he keeps power - and why no one stops him.

TEASERS:

TEASER LINK 1
GOVAN: “He’s a convicted sex offender… and still eligible for re-election.”
KAYLYNN PALM: “It’s a smack in the face… a middle finger to survivors of GBV.”
GOVAN: We uncover the legal loophole that keeps him on the ballot - and the system that refuses to move him off it.

TEASER LINK 2
GOVAN: “In this Klein Karoo municipality, a convicted sex offender still dons the mayoral chain.”
JOSLYN JOHNSON: “We have more potholes than tar on the roads.”
GOVAN: We investigate the structural failures and political loyalties protecting a convicted rapist.

TEASER LINK 3
GOVAN: “He’s a mayor convicted of statutory rape. And he’s running this municipality into the ground.”
JAN-DIRK BRAK: “People have to go and fetch the municipal workers… to fix burst pipes.”
GOVAN: We discover how a convicted sex offender keeps political power - while services collapse around him.

Show me the law!” MASA: ‘It’s still outrageous!’ JEFFREY DONSON: “Bring the law that says I can’t be mayor!” GOVAN: That law - set out in the Constitution and the Municipal Structures Act - disqualifies candidates only when they’ve served more than 12 months in prison without a fine. It applies to statutory rape cases, too. GOVAN: According to the IEC, Donson’s suspended sentence keeps him eligible - as mayor of the worst run municipality in the Western Cape. GOVAN: Engineer Jan-Dirk Brak moved to Ladismith from Cape Town in 2019, looking for a quieter life. Instead, he found a municipality in crisis. GOVAN: “I haven’t seen any municipal leadership or even municipal trucks since the whole day that we’ve been here.” JAN-DIRK BRAK: “So when there’s a callout for a leaky pipe or a power failure or a burst pipe somewhere, in a bunch of cases people have to go and fetch the municipal workers from the facility and take them to the site to fix it.” GOVAN: “Who has to fetch?” JAN-DIRK BRAK: “The business owner or the person living in the house with the problem.” GOVAN: “Has to fetch the municipal worker?” JAN-DIRK BRAK: “Has to go fetch the people from the yard to come do the work…” GOVAN: “Man!” JAN-DIRK BRAK: “And then they’ll pitch up without the required equipment or PPE… it’s not the ampenaar se skuld nie… they don’t have the vehicles or the equipment or the pipe fittings.” GOVAN: Residents are now paying for infrastructure repairs themselves. JAN-DIRK BRAK: “So we had a massive problem with burst pipes about two months ago, and all the fittings were bought by the people in town and donated to the ampenare… because the municipality doesn’t have the money to buy the fittings and the screws and the sealants or whatever’s needed to fix the pipes.” GOVAN: In a province where most municipalities achieved clean or stable audits, Kannaland is the outlier - the worst performer of all 24, with broken finances and collapsing services. GOVAN: Yet even when faced with such obvious decay, why does the broader Kannaland community continue to stand with Donson? GOVAN LINK “Here in Ladismith they didn’t just re-elect Jeffrey Donson; they named a street after him. A convicted child rapist - immortalised in metal and paint.” GOVAN: In Kannaland, voter turnout is shrinking with each election cycle; a small but steady base keeps returning the same result. GOVAN: To them, Donson is the mayor who dances with locals, and feels less like a politician and more like ‘ons se men’s’.” GOVAN: “It‘s Day 2 in Ladismith, Kannaland, and we’re still looking for Jeffrey Donson. We haven’t been able to find him so far, and he’s not responding to our requests for an interview. This is where we spoke to him last time; I’m gonna go try and find him.” GOVAN: “Middag. Howzit, howzit, hey howzit. Is the Mayor in today?” BODYGUARD: “He’s not going to see anyone, he’s busy.” GOVAN: “Sorry?” BODYGUARD: “He doesn’t want to see anybody today.” GOVAN: “Can you tell him that Govan from Carte Blanche is here. We have sent him a number of requests to speak to him.” BODYGUARD: “He doesn’t want to speak to anybody.” GOVAN: “He’s not going to speak to anybody? Can you tell him that we’re here though, just so that he knows we’re here? Just ask him to come and speak to us, we, we, we’re outside.” BODYGUARD: Ja, but he's not going to see anybody today. GOVAN: “Can you ask him to respond to our emails?” BODYGUARD: “Okay, I will tell his PA now.” (inaudible) GOVAN: “So, hy is hier so? Hy is maar hy wil nie saam met ons wil praat?” BODYGUARD: (inaudible) GOVAN: “Okay, dankie.” GOVAN: “Okay, well, that was his bodyguard. He says the Mayor knows we’re here, but has decided he’s not going to speak to anyone today, especially us. He says he doesn’t wanna see us or speak to us. This is the mayor of the worst municipality in the Western Cape, a convicted child rapist. And again, it’s ‘no comment’. It’s unacceptable!” GOVAN: And that’s why there are mounting calls for reform. KAYLYNN PALM: “Look, the voters, I think that they are partly to blame in terms of getting him into power, into this position, continuously…. GOVAN: Kaylynn Palm is from Action Society, a civil rights organisation fighting for a reformed justice system. KAYLYNN PALM: “We also question, not only the voters, but also his colleagues in office. Why do they continuously vote him into stand for, for, for his position?” GOVAN: Action Society wants to keep people with serious convictions - like Donson - out of public office. That means changing the law. GOVAN: “What’s the campaign that Action Society launched?” KAYLYNN PALM: “The campaign focussed on changing legislation which focuses on people who come into office that have a history of serious crimes.” GOVAN: “I’ve heard it being described as the ‘Donson Clause’…” KAYLYNN PALM: “Absolutely, and that is something that we would like to zoom into and have changed, that amendment changed.” GOVAN: Until that happens, Donson is entitled to serve as mayor. Kaylynn says that’s a dangerous message to be sending to victims. KAYLYNN PALM: “I think it’s a smack in the face, and it’s a middle finger to people who are seeking justice for crimes like rape, crimes like sexual assault or GBV.” KAYLYNN PALM: “I’m not sure if he’s just delusional, or if he just, he thinks people must forget what he did. But we can’t forget that he raped a child.”- GOVAN: This story isn’t just about Jeffrey Donson. It’s about a system of public service unable to hold him to account, and a community of close to 30 thousand paying the price. FTB. metadata.Summary: In December 2022, Carte Blanche exposed Kannaland’s scandal-plagued mayor Jeffrey Donson - a convicted child rapist who, despite national outrage, continued to hold public office. Three years later, he’s still there. Convicted in 2008 of statutory rape and indecent assault of a 15-year-old girl while serving as Oudtshoorn’s mayor, Donson has worn the mayoral chain three separate times - before his conviction, again in 2021, and once more in October 2022, just months before our exposé aired. Public pressure forced his temporary removal in January 2022, but coalition politics between ICOSA and the ANCbrought him back. In October 2023, ICOSA suspended him for “gross misconduct and bringing the party into disrepute.” But within weeks, Donson reasserted control - and remains Executive Mayor of Kannaland in 2025. Now, Action Society is pushing for a constitutional amendment to bar convicted sexual offenders from public office - what activists call “the Donson Clause.” October 2025: IDonson remains mayor despite his 2008 conviction and failed suspension. Action Society campaign: Renewed national call to change eligibility laws. Upcoming elections: With local government polls looming in 2026, Donson’s case epitomises the collapse of accountability in local politics. Political stakes: Parties that once backed him - or stayed silent - will now have to answer to voters. National relevance: In a country that preaches “zero tolerance” for GBV, a convicted rapist’s survival in politics exposes the emptiness of that promise. This story isn’t about one small-town scandal - it’s about a democracy without moral guardrails. If a convicted child rapist can outlast exposure, suspension, and scandal - and still run a municipality - what does that say about the system itself? Taxpayers pay his salary. Survivors see justice mocked. Voters are asked to choose between ethics and apathy. As South Africa heads toward another local election, this story shows what’s truly at stake: not just ballots, but belief in the power of accountability.
